title: Investment Company Securities

brief.md:
- Investment company = a **professionally selected and managed pool** of securities sold to retail investors: diversification from a small cheque, professional management, lower risk than a single security.
- Shares are **registered and disclosed under the Securities Act of 1933** like other corporate securities; the entity itself is regulated by the **Investment Company Act of 1940 (1940 Act)**.
- **Three 1940 Act categories**: (1) **face-amount certificate companies** (debt securities; very rare, *not important for the exam*), (2) **unit investment trusts (UITs)**, (3) **management companies** = **closed-end funds** and **open-end funds (mutual funds)**.
- **ETFs** are a hybrid: legally set up as either a **UIT or an open-end fund**.
- **Management company** = hires a professional (an **investment adviser**) to select securities and run the portfolio toward a stated objective. Advisers fall under the **Investment Advisers Act of 1940** and generally must register with the **SEC**.
- **Redeemable** securities (mutual funds, UITs) have **no secondary market**: bought from and sold back to the issuer.
> **Exam tip** Map it: management company (active) = mutual fund + closed-end fund. Not managed = UIT. Hybrid = ETF.

brief.h: Mutual funds: features, disclosure and restrictions
brief.md:
- **Open-end fund** = mutual fund, the **most popular** investment company security. Continuous offering of brand-new, redeemable shares; no limit on shares created.
- Selling points: **professional management, diversification, affordability** (low initial and subsequent purchases), **liquidity** (redeem any time at the next NAV, less any redemption fee).
- Every fund needs a clearly defined **investment objective**, changeable only by a **majority vote of outstanding shares**.
- Reps who sell funds are also subject to the **Securities Exchange Act of 1934**. The SEC sets **disclosure requirements and fee limits** but does **not** supervise investment decisions or judge the merits.
- **Prospectus**: every buyer must receive one. The SEC permits a **summary prospectus** (plain English, usually **10–12 pages** vs ~50 for the full document), delivered **before or at the time of sale**.
- **Seven summary prospectus items**: objectives; fee table; principal strategies, risks and performance; advisers and portfolio managers; buying/selling information; tax information; compensation paid to financial intermediaries.
- If a summary is used, the **full prospectus and supplemental information must be available on request** (paper or electronic). Prospectuses are kept current and **updated annually**.
- **Semiannual financial reports** to shareholders: balance sheet, income statement, portfolio snapshot.
- **Prohibited for funds**: selling **short**, buying on **margin**, **joint** investment or trading accounts. Funds issue **common shares only** (no preferred stock, no bonds).
> **Exam tip** Short, margin, joint accounts, senior securities = all **no** for a mutual fund. A closed-end fund can do all of them.

brief.h: Structure of a mutual fund and who does what
brief.md:
A fund has **no employees**; it relies on affiliated or independent service providers.

| Party | Role |
|---|---|
| **Board of directors** | Required by law; oversees the fund for shareholders, **not day-to-day**. Elected by shareholders. At least **40% independent** directors (no significant business tie to adviser, principal underwriter or affiliates) |
| **Investment adviser** | Hired by the board. Invests cash and securities, implements the board’s objectives, runs **day-to-day trading**. Paid an annual **management fee** (usually a % of NAV). Contract approved **annually** by the board |
| **Custodian** | Bank or trust company that **safekeeps** the fund’s securities and assets |
| **Transfer agent** | Issues, redeems, cancels shares; pays **dividends and capital gains**; sends **trade confirmations**; processes investor mailings |
| **Sponsor** (distributor / underwriter) | Sells the shares. **Annually renewable written contract**; buys from the fund at **NAV**, resells at **POP** (NAV + sales charge) directly or through broker-dealers |

- Custodian and transfer agent are **often the same entity**; both are paid fees by the fund.
- Dealers that distribute need a **written selling agreement** with the sponsor; they buy at a **discount to POP** and fill customer orders at POP.
> **Exam tip** Adviser = invests. Custodian = holds. Transfer agent = records, confirms, pays out. Sponsor = sells.

- Three ways to earn: **dividend payments** (net of fund expenses), **capital gains distributions** (net of losses, paid at year-end), **NAV increases**.
- Tax is owed on **net investment income**: dividends, interest and net capital gains.
- Categories: **money market, stock, bond, asset allocation** (actively managed) plus **index funds** (passive). The customer’s **objectives** matter more than fund size, fees or policies when choosing.
- **Money market funds**: safest and most stable; 1940 Act limits holdings to high-quality, liquid debt with **remaining maturity ≤ 13 months** (T-bills, commercial paper, negotiable CDs). Aim for **$1 NAV** but *not guaranteed* (**breaking the buck**). Typically **no-load**. Fit: safety, stability, liquidity; poor at beating inflation.
- **Stock funds**: long-term growth. **Large-cap** (often > $10 billion, blue chip, relatively stable) vs **small-cap** (roughly $750 million–$2 billion, more upside and risk). **Growth** (rarely pays dividends), **income** (preferred, blue chip, utility stocks), **growth and income / combination**, **international / global** (global may include US firms; emerging markets add risk and reward), **sector / specialty** (concentrated, riskier).
- **Bond funds** (fixed-income): income. **US government** (lowest credit risk, lowest yield), **corporate**, **high-yield / junk** (below investment grade, higher default risk, higher yield), **municipal** (tax-exempt; for high-bracket investors). Longer average maturity = more **NAV volatility** and higher yield; fund value moves **inversely with rates**. Risks: default, interest rate, reinvestment rate.
- **Asset allocation funds**: mix of stocks (growth), bonds (income), cash (safety); manager has some discretion to shift the mix.
- **Index funds**: the **only mutual fund type not actively managed**; hold most or all securities of an index (S&P 500). Low fees, tax-efficient, will not beat the market. **Wilshire 5000** = actively traded US companies; **Russell Top 50 Mega Cap** = 50 largest stocks in the Russell 3000.
> **Exam tip** Muni fund: the **dividends** are tax-exempt, **capital gains distributions are taxable**.

- **NAV** = total assets − total liabilities. **NAV per share** = NAV ÷ shares outstanding. Open-end funds must compute it **at least once every business day** (typically at the exchange close, **4:00 pm ET**).
- Selling or redeeming shares does **not** change NAV per share. A **distribution** (dividend) **lowers NAV** by the amount paid.
- **Forward pricing**: buy and redemption orders get the **next NAV calculated** after the order is received. Not the prior close, not the next open.
- **Redemption**: fund must pay within **7 calendar days**. Proceeds = NAV less any redemption fee or deferred sales charge. There is **no secondary market**, so mutual funds do not suit someone who wants **intraday trading**.
- **Undivided interest**: each holder owns a proportionate share of every portfolio security.
- **Average cost basis** = total cost of all shares ÷ total shares owned. Available for **mutual fund** redemptions, **not** for shares of specific stocks. Gain/loss = redemption price − average cost.
- **Margin**: mutual fund shares cannot be bought on margin (**100% cash**). After **30 days** they acquire **loan value** and may serve as collateral.
> **Exam tip** Order at 5:00 pm Monday = Tuesday’s NAV. No order ever executes at a price the investor already knows.

brief.h: Sales charges, 12b-1 fees and the expense ratio
brief.md:
- **Sales charge (load)** compensates the salesperson; paid once (front-end) or on exit (back-end/CDSC) or level, depending on share class.
- **POP = NAV + sales charge.** The sales charge is always a **percentage of POP, never of NAV**.
- **Sales charge % = (POP − NAV) ÷ POP.** Shortcut: **POP = NAV ÷ (1 − sales charge %)**.
- **Maximum sales charge**: **8.5% of POP** if the fund offers **all three** features (breakpoints, rights of accumulation, reinvestment at NAV); otherwise **6.25%**. Competition usually pushes actual charges lower.
- **12b-1 fee**: annual marketing and distribution/administrative cost; **not** management fees or trading costs. **Maximum 0.75%** of average net assets; a fund calling itself **no-load** can charge **no more than 0.25%**. Must be approved initially and **annually** by **shareholders and the board**.
- **Expense ratio** = (management fees + operating expenses) ÷ average annual net assets. Disclosed prominently in the prospectus. Actively managed: about **0.5%–1.0%**; index funds: usually **0.25% or less**. It rises if expenses grow faster than assets.
- **No-load**: sold at NAV (NAV = POP), usually directly from the fund company; no sales charge. Index funds are typically no-load.
> **Exam tip** Management fees sit inside the expense ratio, not inside 12b-1. The sales charge is not in the expense ratio either.

| Class | Charge structure | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | **Front-end** load paid at purchase | **Lowest 12b-1**; the **only class with breakpoints**; suits long holders and large purchases |
| **B** | **Back-end / CDSC** paid on redemption within a set number of years | **Higher 12b-1 than A**; **no breakpoints**; suits small amounts and a long horizon |
| **C** | **Level load** (front- or back-end) | **Relatively high 12b-1** and other annual costs = **highest annual expenses**; **no breakpoints**; suits **short-term** holders; costs grow the longer you hold |
| **No-load** | None; NAV = POP | Bought directly from the fund company |

- Typical B-share CDSC schedule: **5%, 4%, 3%, 3%, 2%, 1%, then 0 from year 7**. The CDSC **declines** and is paid once, on redemption; it is **not** an annual charge.
- **All share classes carry 12b-1 fees**.
- Multi-class structures let investors match fee structure to time horizon.
> **Exam tip** Breakpoints = Class A only. Long horizon + small cheque = B. Short horizon = C.

brief.h: Breakpoints, letters of intent, rights of accumulation, reinvestment
brief.md:
- **Breakpoint** = a discount on the sales charge for larger dollar amounts; schedule is in the prospectus. Example schedule: under $50k = 5.75%; $50k–$99,999 = 4.50%; $100k–$249,999 = 3.50%; $250k–$499,999 = 2.50%.
- Breakpoints apply to the **entire purchase**, **not incrementally**. $350,000 at the schedule above = **2.5% on all $350,000**.
- **Breakpoint sale** = recommending a purchase just **below** a breakpoint to earn a higher commission. **Prohibited**.
- **Letter of intent (LOI)**: written promise to invest a stated total within **13 months**; every purchase gets the sales charge of the **promised total**. Can be **backdated 90 days**. Can cover accounts of **spouse and minor children**. Shares bought at the reduced charge sit in **escrow**; if the target is missed the extra shares are **liquidated to pay the higher charge**. **Appreciation, reinvested dividends and capital gains do not count** toward an LOI.
- **Rights of accumulation (ROA)**: discount on **subsequent purchases** based on the total position (not the first purchase). **No time limit**, and **appreciation and reinvested dividends count**.
- **Combination purchase**: aggregate holdings across the **same fund family**; **spouse and minor children** can combine too.
- **Reinvestment at NAV**: dividends and gains reinvested with **no sales charge**. Offering breakpoints + ROA + NAV reinvestment is what allows the **8.5%** maximum.
- Taxes: reinvesting does **not avoid tax** (taxed when accrued). Reinvested amounts **raise cost basis** (e.g., $1,000 basis + $200 reinvested = $1,200).
> **Exam tip** LOI = future promise (13 months, 90-day backdate). ROA = looks at what you already hold, no time limit.

- **Late trading**: filling orders received **after the close** at **that day’s** price instead of the next NAV. Prohibited because after-close news gives an information advantage. NAV is usually struck at **4:00 pm ET**; later orders get the **next business day’s** NAV (forward pricing).
- **Switching** (also called churning in the book): moving a customer between funds with **similar objectives for no legitimate purpose**. Creates extra costs and tax. Example: one growth fund into another near-identical growth fund.
- **Selling dividends**: selling a fund **just before it pays a dividend**. The dividend lowers NAV and creates a **taxable event**, so the customer pays tax on money that is just a return of their own purchase price.
  - Example: NAV $10, $1 dividend coming. Buy at $10, receive $1 (taxable), NAV falls to $9. Buying after the payment at $9 avoids the tax.
- **Breakpoint sale** (see previous section) is also a prohibited practice.
> **Exam tip** All four are about *timing or structuring the sale for the rep’s benefit*, not the client’s.

- A management company with a **fixed number of shares** and fixed capital. Shares are issued through an **IPO** (additional public offerings possible), then **trade on an exchange investor-to-investor**. The fund does **not redeem** shares, so it never has to sell holdings in a falling market to meet redemptions.
- Same advantages as mutual funds: professional management, diversification, affordability, liquidity; also pays dividends and capital gains.
- **Pricing**: has an NAV but need not compute it daily. Market price set by **supply and demand**, so it can trade **above (premium), at, or below (discount)** NAV.
  - Offer price **below NAV** means the product **must be a closed-end fund** (a mutual fund is never offered below NAV).
- **Costs**: pays **commissions** on buy and sell; **no sales charge, no 12b-1 fee**; still has an annual **expense ratio**.
- Trades like a stock: market, limit and stop orders; executes in minutes during the day; **intraday trading**. A *buy at NAV* order does not exist.
- **Can be bought on margin and sold short.**
- **Capital raising**: may issue **senior securities** (preferred stock, bonds) and **borrow/leverage**; a mutual fund cannot.
- Single share class (no A/B/C).
> **Exam tip** Intraday trader = closed-end fund or ETF. Commission = closed-end fund or ETF. Sales charge = mutual fund.

- Created by a **sponsor** drafting a **trust indenture** that names a **trustee**. Trustee handles **custody, recordkeeping, accounting and tax reporting**.
- **No board of directors, no corporate officers, no investment adviser**. **Not actively managed**: the portfolio is **fixed and supervised**, not traded.
- Can hold fixed-income (corporate, international, agency, municipal) or equities. The sponsor may remove or add securities only in limited cases listed in the prospectus: **severe credit downgrade, bankruptcy, fraud, merger or acquisition**.
- Benefits: **no style drift**, known holdings (listed in the prospectus), **cheaper than mutual funds** (no active management fee), **tax efficient**, predictable (often **monthly**) distributions that can be reinvested, accurate expected yield for bond UITs.
- **Fixed termination date** set at creation (bond UIT often tied to maturities, 20–30 years; equity UIT may be a year or a few). At termination, assets are sold and proceeds distributed.
- **Units** sold once in an **IPO** (a prospectus is required). Redeemable with the trust, priced **end of each business day**; **no secondary market**. Redemption value may be more or less than cost. Some UITs allow exchange into another UIT at a **reduced sales charge**. More units can reach the market only when others are redeemed.
- Risks: not suited to **capital preservation**; takes the risk of the underlying securities; no guarantee of objective or of getting back cost.
> **Exam tip** UIT = fixed portfolio **and** fixed termination date. ETFs have neither a termination date nor a truly fixed portfolio.

brief.h: Exchange-traded funds and the four-way comparison
brief.md:
- **ETF** = exchange-traded investment company designed to **track a benchmark, sector or index** (stocks, bonds, commodities such as gold or oil). Legally a **UIT or an open-end fund**.
- **Passive**: portfolio changes only when the **index changes** (the process of adding/removing securities to mirror the index is **reconstitution**). The exam treats ETFs as passive.
- **Trades like a stock**: priced by supply and demand, **premium or discount to NAV**, intraday, **commissions** paid, **short selling, margin, limit and stop orders** all available.
- **Pros**: low expense ratio, tax-efficient (low turnover, few realised gains), very liquid.
- **Cons**: commissions erode returns; easy liquidity can lead to **overtrading and timing risk**; returns match but do not beat the benchmark.

| Feature | Mutual fund | Closed-end | UIT | ETF |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Shares | Continuous offering | Fixed, IPO | Fixed, one-time IPO | Fixed, IPO |
| Redeemed at NAV | Yes | No | Yes | No |
| Exchange trading | No | Yes | No | Yes |
| Management | Active | Active | Supervised, fixed | Supervised (passive) |
| Termination date | No | No | **Yes** | No |
| Sales charge / commission | Sales charge, 12b-1 | Commission | Sales charge | Commission |
| Margin / short | No | Yes | Not covered in the book | Yes |

- Closed-end and ETFs trade **intraday**; mutual funds and UITs do not. Secondary-market trading = more liquid.
- Active management = higher fees; closed-end and mutual funds are active, UITs and ETFs are **supervised**.
> **Exam tip** When the question says *fixed number of shares*, think closed-end/ETF/UIT; *continuous offering* is mutual fund only.

traps: **Redeemed vs traded.** Mutual funds and UITs are **redeemed** by the issuer at NAV (no secondary market). Closed-end funds and ETFs **trade** investor-to-investor on an exchange at a market price that can differ from NAV.
**Sales charge is a percentage of POP, not NAV.** NAV $20 with a 5% load is *not* $21. POP = NAV ÷ (1 − 0.05) = $21.05. Mutual funds always describe the load against POP.

**Forward pricing vs late trading.** An order after the 4:00 pm close gets the **next** NAV. Filling it at the same day’s price is **late trading**, a violation. Never the prior close, never the next open.

**Custodian vs transfer agent vs adviser vs sponsor.** Custodian *holds* assets; transfer agent *issues/cancels shares, mails confirms, pays distributions*; adviser *invests and trades*; sponsor *sells shares*.
**Muni bond fund tax.** Dividends (tax-free interest) are exempt from federal tax; **capital gains distributions are taxable**. The tax break covers interest only.
**Money market fund promises.** The $1 NAV is a target, not a guarantee (breaking the buck). It is **not FDIC insured**, even though similar names exist at banks. It is also typically **no-load**.

**Index fund vs UIT vs ETF.** Index mutual funds are redeemable and have no exchange trading; ETFs trade intraday; UITs have a **termination date**. None of the three is actively managed to beat the market.
**Reinvestment avoids sales charge, not tax.** Dividends reinvested at NAV are still taxed when accrued, and they **increase cost basis**, so they should not be taxed again at sale.

**Rights of accumulation vs letter of intent.** ROA looks backward at the existing position (no time limit, appreciation counts, subsequent purchases only). LOI is a forward promise (13 months, 90-day backdate, appreciation does **not** count).
**Breakpoints are not incremental.** The lower sales charge applies to the **whole** purchase once the threshold is reached, and breakpoints exist only for **Class A**.
**12b-1 vs management fee.** 12b-1 covers marketing and distribution only, max 0.75%, and 0.25% for a fund to call itself no-load. Management fees are separate and sit in the expense ratio.
**8.5% vs 6.25%.** The 8.5% cap needs breakpoints, rights of accumulation and NAV reinvestment. Without all three the cap is 6.25%.
**What changes NAV per share.** A distribution **lowers** it. Buying or redeeming shares does **not**. Market moves of the portfolio change it daily.

**Margin and mutual funds.** The fund itself cannot buy on margin or sell short; investors cannot buy fund shares on margin (100% cash) but can use shares held **30 days** as collateral. Closed-end shares and ETFs *can* be bought on margin.
**Commission vs sales charge.** Closed-end funds and ETFs: **commission**. Mutual funds: **sales charge** (plus possible 12b-1). UITs: sales charge. Closed-end funds never charge 12b-1.

**Board independence vs adviser contract.** At least **40%** of directors must be independent; the adviser’s contract is approved **annually** by the board; a sponsor’s contract is **annually renewable**. Do not swap numbers or parties.

**Pricing relationship clues.** If the offer price is **below** NAV, it cannot be a mutual fund (closed-end only). If it equals NAV, it could be either (a no-load mutual fund or a closed-end fund). Above NAV could be either.

**Switching vs breakpoint sale vs selling dividends.** Switching = pointless move between similar funds; breakpoint sale = deal sized just under a discount; selling dividends = purchase timed just before a payout. All are prohibited.

formulas.name: NAV and NAV per share
formulas.rule: NAV = total assets − total liabilities.  NAV per share = NAV ÷ shares outstanding.  A distribution lowers NAV by the amount paid; buys and redemptions do not change NAV per share.
formulas.example: Assets $250M, liabilities $30M → NAV $220M. With 11M shares: 220 ÷ 11 = **$20.00** per share. A $0.80 dividend moves it to **$19.20**.

formulas.name: POP and sales charge
formulas.rule: POP = NAV + sales charge.  Sales charge % = (POP − NAV) ÷ POP.  POP = NAV ÷ (1 − sales charge %).  Load is always a % of POP.

formulas.name: Expense ratio
formulas.rule: Expense ratio = (management fees + operating expenses) ÷ average annual net assets.  Sales charges are not included.  Active ≈ 0.5%–1.0%; index ≤ 0.25%.
formulas.example: Management fees $4M + operating expenses $1M = $5M ÷ average net assets $400M = **1.25%**.

formulas.name: Average cost basis
formulas.rule: Average cost = total dollars paid for all shares ÷ total shares owned.  Gain or loss = redemption price − average cost.  Reinvested distributions add to total cost.

formulas.name: Breakpoint sales charge (whole purchase)
formulas.rule: Find the bracket for the total purchase and apply that rate to **all** dollars. LOI: use the rate of the promised total on every purchase within 13 months (backdate up to 90 days).
formulas.example: Book schedule, $350,000 purchase → 2.5% × 350,000 = **$8,750**. LOI for $125,000 with $10,000 first purchase → **3.50%** on that $10,000 = $350.

formulas.name: Distribution effect and cost basis
formulas.rule: NAV after distribution = NAV before − distribution per share.  Reinvested distribution increases cost basis by the amount reinvested (it was already taxed).
formulas.example: NAV $10, $1 dividend → NAV **$9**. Basis $1,000 + $200 reinvested dividends = **$1,200**.

formulas.name: Open-end vs closed-end price test
formulas.rule: Offer price < NAV → closed-end only.  Offer price = NAV → no-load mutual fund or closed-end.  Offer price > NAV → mutual fund with load or closed-end at a premium.
formulas.example: NAV $10, offer $9 → closed-end. NAV $10, offer $11 → either. NAV $10, offer $10 → either (no-load if mutual).

formulas.name: Four-way comparison: who has what
formulas.rule: Continuous offering: MF only. Redeemed at NAV: MF, UIT. Exchange trading and commissions: CEF, ETF. Active management: MF, CEF. Termination date: UIT only. Margin and short: CEF, ETF.
formulas.example: Client wants intraday trading, lower costs, index exposure → **ETF**. Client wants predictable monthly income, fixed holdings, set end date → **UIT**.
