cards.f: Which law regulates investment companies?
cards.b: The **Investment Company Act of 1940**. Their shares are also registered under the Securities Act of 1933.

cards.f: The three 1940 Act categories of investment companies
cards.b: **Face-amount certificate companies, unit investment trusts (UITs), management companies** (closed-end and open-end funds).

cards.f: Which investment company category is not important for the exam?
cards.b: **Face-amount certificate companies** (issue debt; very few exist).

cards.f: Open-end fund is another name for…
cards.b: A **mutual fund**, the most popular investment company security.

cards.f: What is a management company?
cards.b: An investment company that hires an **investment adviser** to actively select and manage the portfolio toward a stated objective.

cards.f: Which law governs investment advisers?
cards.b: **Investment Advisers Act of 1940**; advisers generally register with the SEC.

cards.f: What does redeemable mean for a fund security?
cards.b: **No secondary market**: bought from and sold back to the issuer (mutual funds, UITs).

cards.f: How can a mutual fund’s investment objective be changed?
cards.b: Only by a **majority vote of outstanding shares**.

cards.f: Four selling points of mutual funds
cards.b: **Professional management, diversification, affordability, liquidity.**

cards.f: Does the SEC judge a fund’s investment merits?
cards.b: **No.** It sets disclosure rules and fee limits but does not supervise investment decisions or judge merits.

cards.f: How long is a summary prospectus versus a full prospectus?
cards.b: Summary about **10–12 pages**; full about **50 pages**.

cards.f: When may a summary prospectus be delivered?
cards.b: **Prior to or at the time of sale.** The full prospectus must remain available on request.

cards.f: How often must a prospectus be updated?
cards.b: **Annually.**

cards.f: How often do shareholders get financial reports, and what is in them?
cards.b: **Semiannually**: balance sheet, income statement, portfolio snapshot.

cards.f: Name the seven summary prospectus items
cards.b: Objectives; fee table; strategies/risks/performance; advisers and managers; buying/selling info; **tax info**; **intermediary compensation**.

cards.f: Minimum share of independent directors on a fund board
cards.b: At least **40%**.

cards.f: What does a fund’s board of directors do?
cards.b: Oversees management and operations for shareholders; **not day-to-day**. Elected by shareholders; hires the adviser.

cards.f: Investment adviser duties
cards.b: **Invests cash and securities, implements the board’s objectives, manages day-to-day trading.**

cards.f: How is the investment adviser paid, and how often is the contract approved?
cards.b: Annual **management fee** (typically % of NAV); contract approved **annually** by the board.

cards.f: Custodian role
cards.b: Bank or trust company that **safekeeps** the fund’s securities and assets.

cards.f: Three transfer agent duties
cards.b: **Issue/redeem/cancel shares; distribute dividends and capital gains; send trade confirmations.**

cards.f: Who is the sponsor of a mutual fund?
cards.b: The **distributor / underwriter** that sells the shares; annually renewable written contract; buys at **NAV**.

cards.f: What do dealers need to sell a fund, and at what price do they buy?
cards.b: A **written selling agreement** with the sponsor; they buy at a **discount to POP**.

cards.f: Three activities mutual funds may not do
cards.b: **Sell short, buy on margin, participate in joint investment/trading accounts.**

cards.f: What types of shares can a mutual fund issue?
cards.b: **Common shares only**; no preferred stock or bonds (no senior securities).

cards.f: Three ways a mutual fund investor earns money
cards.b: **Dividends, capital gains distributions, NAV increases.**

cards.f: What income does a mutual fund investor pay tax on?
cards.b: **Net investment income**: dividends, interest and net capital gains (gains minus losses).

cards.f: What matters most when picking a fund for a client?
cards.b: The customer’s **investment objectives**; fund size is less important than objectives, fees, policies.

cards.f: Maximum remaining maturity for money market fund holdings
cards.b: **13 months.**

cards.f: What is breaking the buck?
cards.b: A money market fund NAV falling **below $1**; the stable $1 is a goal, not a guarantee.

cards.f: Money market fund sales load?
cards.b: Typically **no-load** (no sales charge to buy or redeem).

cards.f: Large-cap vs small-cap fund size ranges in the book
cards.b: Large-cap often above **$10 billion**; small-cap roughly **$750 million–$2 billion**.

cards.f: Which stock fund type rarely pays dividends?
cards.b: **Growth fund** (reinvests earnings; greater upside, risk and volatility).

cards.f: Why are sector funds riskier?
cards.b: They **concentrate** in one industry; one year’s top sector can crash the next.

cards.f: Which bond fund has the lowest credit risk and lowest yield?
cards.b: **US government bond fund.**

cards.f: Who benefits most from a municipal bond fund?
cards.b: **High-net-worth investors in a high tax bracket.**

cards.f: Muni bond fund: which distributions are taxable?
cards.b: **Capital gains distributions** are taxable; the interest dividends are tax-exempt.

cards.f: Longer bond fund maturity means…
cards.b: **Higher yield but greater NAV volatility**; value moves inversely with rates.

cards.f: Three risks of bond funds
cards.b: **Default risk, interest rate risk, reinvestment rate risk.**

cards.f: What is an asset allocation fund?
cards.b: Mix of **stocks (growth), bonds (income), cash (safety)**; manager can shift the mix.

cards.f: Which mutual fund type is not actively managed?
cards.b: **Index fund.**

cards.f: Why are index funds cheaper and more tax-efficient?
cards.b: Little trading: **low management fees**, fewer taxable capital gains.

cards.f: Wilshire 5000 measures…
cards.b: The value of **US companies with actively traded stock.**

cards.f: Russell Top 50 Mega Cap Index tracks…
cards.b: The **50 largest stocks** in the Russell 3000 universe.

cards.f: Formula for NAV
cards.b: **Total assets − total liabilities**; per share = NAV ÷ shares outstanding.

cards.f: How often must an open-end fund compute NAV?
cards.b: **At least once every business day**, typically after the exchanges close.

cards.f: Does selling new shares change NAV per share?
cards.b: **No.** Cash in is offset by new shares. Same for redemptions.

cards.f: Effect of a distribution on NAV
cards.b: NAV **decreases by the amount of the distribution.**

cards.f: Public offering price formula
cards.b: **POP = NAV + sales charge**, or NAV ÷ (1 − sales charge %).

cards.f: How fast must a fund pay redemption proceeds?
cards.b: Within **7 calendar days.**

cards.f: What is forward pricing?
cards.b: Orders are priced at the **next NAV calculated** after receipt.

cards.f: A Monday 5:00 pm buy order gets which price?
cards.b: The NAV calculated **after that order**: Tuesday’s close.

cards.f: Average cost basis formula
cards.b: **Total cost of all shares ÷ total shares owned.** Allowed for mutual fund redemptions, not specific stocks.

cards.f: When do mutual fund shares gain loan value in a margin account?
cards.b: After being held **30 days.**

cards.f: Can mutual fund shares be bought on margin?
cards.b: **No**; 100% cash required.

cards.f: Is a mutual fund sales charge a percentage of NAV or POP?
cards.b: Always of **POP**, never NAV.

cards.f: Maximum front-end sales charge with all three privileges
Maximum sales charge without breakpoints, ROA and NAV reinvestment
What does a 12b-1 fee cover?
cards.b: **Marketing and administrative/distribution** costs; not management fees or trading.

cards.f: Maximum 12b-1 fee, and the cap for a fund advertising as no-load
cards.b: **0.75%** of average net assets; **0.25%** for no-load.

cards.f: Who must approve a 12b-1 fee?
cards.b: Both **shareholders and the board**, originally and annually.

cards.f: Expense ratio formula
cards.b: **(Management fees + operating expenses) ÷ average annual net assets.**

cards.f: Typical expense ratios: active vs index
cards.b: Active about **0.5%–1.0%**; index usually **0.25% or less**.

cards.f: When does an expense ratio rise?
cards.b: When operating expenses grow **faster than the value of investments.**

cards.f: Class A shares: charge and special feature
cards.b: **Front-end load**, lowest 12b-1, the **only class with breakpoints.**

cards.f: Class B shares: charge structure
cards.b: **Back-end / CDSC** on redemption within set years; higher 12b-1 than A; **no breakpoints**.

cards.f: Typical B-share CDSC schedule
Class C shares: charge and best use
cards.b: **Level load**, high annual costs (highest); suits **short-term** holders; no breakpoints.

cards.f: How do you recognise a no-load fund?
cards.b: **NAV equals the purchase price** (NAV = POP).

cards.f: Do breakpoints apply incrementally?
cards.b: **No**; the lower charge applies to the **entire purchase**.

cards.f: What is a breakpoint sale?
cards.b: Recommending a purchase **just below a breakpoint** for higher commission; prohibited.

cards.f: Letter of intent: period and backdating
cards.b: **13 months**, backdated up to **90 days.**

cards.f: What happens if an LOI is not completed?
cards.b: Higher normal charge applies; extra shares held in **escrow** are liquidated to cover it.

cards.f: Do appreciation and reinvested dividends count toward an LOI?
Rights of accumulation: three features
cards.b: **Subsequent purchases only; no time limit; appreciation and reinvested dividends count.**

cards.f: Who can combine purchases for a breakpoint?
cards.b: Same **fund family**; **spouses and minor children.**

cards.f: Does reinvesting dividends at NAV avoid tax?
cards.b: **No.** Tax is owed when accrued; reinvested amounts **raise cost basis.**

cards.f: Define late trading
cards.b: Filling orders received **after the close** at that day’s price instead of the next NAV; NAV usually struck at **4:00 pm ET**.

cards.f: Define switching
cards.b: Moving a client between funds with **similar objectives** with no legitimate purpose.

cards.f: Why is selling dividends harmful?
cards.b: Dividend **lowers NAV** and triggers a **taxable event** on money the client just paid in.

cards.f: Closed-end fund share count and how it is sold
cards.b: **Fixed number**, sold in an **IPO**, then traded on an exchange.

cards.f: Why does a closed-end fund not need ready liquidity?
cards.b: It **does not redeem shares**, so no forced sales in a falling market.

cards.f: Must a closed-end fund compute NAV daily?
cards.b: **No**; price is set by supply and demand and can be above or below NAV.

cards.f: Offer price below NAV tells you which product?
cards.b: A **closed-end fund** (a mutual fund is never offered below NAV).

cards.f: Closed-end fund costs for investors
cards.b: **Commission** on buy and sell; **no sales charge, no 12b-1**; has annual expense ratio.

cards.f: Which orders work for closed-end shares?
cards.b: Market, limit and stop, as with stocks. A buy-at-NAV order does not exist.

cards.f: Can closed-end funds issue preferred stock, bonds or borrow?
cards.b: **Yes**; mutual funds cannot.

cards.f: Can closed-end shares be bought on margin or sold short?
cards.b: **Yes** (mutual funds: no).

cards.f: Document that creates a UIT
cards.b: The **trust indenture**, drafted by the sponsor, naming a trustee.

cards.f: What does a UIT trustee do?
cards.b: Custody of securities, recordkeeping for investors, **accounting and tax reporting.**

cards.f: What does a UIT not have?
cards.b: No **board of directors, corporate officers or investment adviser.**

cards.f: Reasons a UIT sponsor may change the portfolio
cards.b: **Severe credit decline, bankruptcy, fraud, merger/acquisition requirement.**

cards.f: Is a UIT portfolio actively traded?
cards.b: No: **supervised, not traded.**

cards.f: UIT termination date is set when?
cards.b: At **creation**; tied to the securities (bond maturities, or a year or few for stocks).

cards.f: When are UIT units sold, and how do holders exit?
cards.b: Units are sold in an **IPO only**; exit by **redemption** with the trust (no secondary market).

cards.f: UIT redemption pricing
cards.b: Priced at the **end of each business day** at current underlying value.

cards.f: UIT benefits
cards.b: **Fixed known holdings, low cost, tax efficient, predictable monthly distributions, set end date.**

cards.f: UIT unsuitable for which goal?
cards.b: **Capital preservation**; no guarantee of value at termination.

cards.f: ETF legal structures
cards.b: Either a **UIT or an open-end fund.**

cards.f: When does an ETF portfolio change?
cards.b: Only when the **underlying index changes** (reconstitution).

cards.f: ETF trading features
cards.b: Premium/discount to NAV; **intraday**; commissions; short sales, margin, limit and stop orders.

cards.f: ETF disadvantages
cards.b: **Commissions, overtrading/timing risk, no outperformance of the benchmark.**

cards.f: Which products trade intraday on the secondary market?
cards.b: **Closed-end funds and ETFs**; not mutual funds or UITs.

cards.f: Which product has both a fixed portfolio and a termination date?
cards.b: The **UIT** only.

cards.f: Which product has a continuous offering of shares?
cards.b: The **mutual fund** only.

cards.f: What does ‘undivided interest’ mean for a mutual fund shareholder?
cards.b: Each holder owns a **proportionate share of every security** in the portfolio, not particular holdings.

cards.f: Components of a fund’s total return
cards.b: **Change in NAV, dividend payments and capital gains distributions.** NAV alone understates the return.

cards.f: Are money market mutual funds FDIC insured?
cards.b: **Never.** Bank money market deposit accounts can be insured; the similar-sounding mutual funds are not.

cards.f: Bond fund for low tolerance of share-value swings but a need for income
cards.b: A **short-term bond fund**; longer-term funds yield more but swing more with rates.

cards.f: Why are money market funds a poor fit for inflation protection?
cards.b: Their returns are **relatively low**; they suit safety, stability and liquidity, not keeping pace with inflation.

cards.f: Which mutual fund features are shared by closed-end funds, UITs and ETFs?
cards.b: **Diversification, low minimum investment and a clearly stated objective.** Only mutual funds offer a continuous offering of new shares and breakpoints.

cards.f: Can a UIT investor move to another trust cheaply?
cards.b: Some UITs allow an **exchange into a different UIT at a reduced sales charge**.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three categories of investment company recognized by the Investment Company Act of 1940?
w: Correct: a real estate operating company is not a 1940 Act investment company category, so it is the exception.
Wrong: unit investment trusts are expressly one of the three categories regulated by the 1940 Act.
Wrong: management companies, covering both open-end and closed-end funds, are a core 1940 Act category.
Wrong: face-amount certificate companies are one of the three 1940 Act categories, even though they are rare today.

questions.q: A customer asks how she will eventually sell mutual fund shares she is about to buy. Which statement is accurate?
o: She will sell them to another investor on the NYSE
She will sell them back to the issuing fund, because there is no secondary market
She will sell them to the sponsor at the public offering price
She will place a limit order that executes at a price she specifies
w: Wrong: mutual fund shares do not trade on an exchange; that is how closed-end funds and ETFs work.
Correct: mutual fund shares are redeemable, so they are sold back to the fund with no investor-to-investor market.
Wrong: redemption is at NAV (less any fees), not at the public offering price that includes a sales charge.
Wrong: limit orders belong to exchange-traded products; mutual fund orders are priced at the next calculated NAV.

questions.q: A fund’s representative hands a prospective investor a summary prospectus at the time of sale. Which statement is correct?
o: The summary prospectus must be replaced by a full prospectus within seven calendar days
The delivery is improper because the full prospectus must always be delivered before the sale
The fund must also make the full prospectus and supplemental information available on request
The summary prospectus is acceptable only for funds with no sales charge
w: Wrong: no rule requires replacing the summary with the full document within seven days; seven days relates to redemption payments.
Wrong: the SEC permits delivering a summary prospectus prior to or at the time of sale, so delivery here is proper.
Correct: the SEC allows a summary prospectus, but the fund must make the full document available on request, on paper or electronically.
Wrong: the summary prospectus option is not restricted by whether a fund has a sales charge.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the items included in a mutual fund summary prospectus?
o: Compensation paid to financial intermediaries for selling the fund
The fund’s complete audited financial statements
w: Wrong: the fee table is one of the seven key items a summary prospectus must cover.
Wrong: compensation paid to financial intermediaries is one of the seven items listed in the summary prospectus.
Wrong: tax information is among the seven required summary prospectus items.
Correct: financial statements belong to the longer, full prospectus; the 10–12 page summary does not carry them.

questions.q: How often must a mutual fund send financial reports (balance sheet, income statement and portfolio snapshot) to its shareholders?
w: Wrong: quarterly is not the schedule the chapter gives for fund shareholder reports; the requirement is twice a year.
Wrong: the prospectus is updated annually, but the financial reports are required more often, twice a year.
Correct: mutual funds must send shareholders financial reports semiannually, meaning twice a year.
Wrong: monthly reports are not required of mutual funds under the chapter’s rules.

questions.q: At least what percentage of a mutual fund’s board of directors must be independent of the fund’s adviser, principal underwriter and affiliates?
w: Wrong: 25% falls below the minimum the 1940 Act sets for independent directors.
Correct: the 1940 Act requires at least 40% of the directors to be independent watchdogs of the fund’s management.
Wrong: a simple majority is a plausible guess but is not the required minimum in the chapter.
Wrong: 75% is far higher than the minimum required for independent directors.

questions.q:
Which of the following are responsibilities of a mutual fund’s investment adviser?

I. Managing day-to-day trading of the portfolio
II. Safekeeping the fund’s securities
III. Implementing the investment objectives set by the board
IV. Issuing and cancelling fund shares
w: Correct: the adviser runs daily trading and carries out the board’s objectives; custody and share issuance belong to others.
Wrong: safekeeping is the custodian’s job and issuing or cancelling shares is the transfer agent’s job.
Wrong: item II is the custodian’s role, so pairing it with trading does not describe the adviser.
Wrong: item IV is a transfer agent function, so this pairing wrongly credits the adviser with it.

questions.q: A shareholder in a mutual fund has not received her year-end capital gains distribution. Which service provider is responsible for distributing dividends and capital gains to shareholders?
w: Wrong: the custodian only holds the fund’s securities in safekeeping and does not pay out distributions.
Wrong: the board oversees the fund generally and is not involved in day-to-day payment mechanics.
Wrong: the adviser invests the portfolio and trades, but does not process shareholder payments.
Correct: the transfer agent issues and redeems shares, sends confirmations and handles dividend and capital gains payouts.

questions.q: A mutual fund sponsor (distributor) normally buys fund shares from the fund at ______ and resells them to the public at ______.
o: the public offering price; net asset value
net asset value less a discount; net asset value
net asset value; the public offering price
the public offering price; the public offering price plus the 12b-1 fee
w: Wrong: this reverses the flow; the sponsor’s margin comes from selling above the price it pays.
Wrong: the sponsor does not get a discount to NAV; the discount to POP applies to dealers buying from the sponsor.
Correct: the sponsor buys at NAV and resells at POP, which is NAV plus the sales charge.
Wrong: the 12b-1 fee is an annual charge, not part of the public offering price.

questions.q: Which of the following activities is a mutual fund permitted to engage in?
o: Redeeming its own shares directly from investors
Issuing preferred stock to raise capital
w: Wrong: the SEC generally prohibits mutual funds from selling securities short.
Correct: redeeming shares directly from investors is what open-end funds do; they have no secondary market.
Wrong: mutual funds may not buy securities with borrowed funds on margin.
Wrong: mutual funds are limited to a single class of common shares and cannot issue senior securities.

questions.q:
Which of the following activities are generally prohibited for a mutual fund?

I. Selling securities short
II. Participating in joint investment or trading accounts
III. Redeeming its shares within seven calendar days
IV. Buying securities on margin
w: Wrong: this omits buying on margin, which is also on the prohibited list for mutual funds.
Wrong: item III is a requirement, and this combination also drops the prohibited joint-account activity.
Wrong: redemption within seven days is required of mutual funds, not prohibited, so including it is incorrect.
Correct: short selling, joint accounts and margin purchases are barred, while redeeming shares promptly is an obligation.

questions.q: The 1940 Act limits money market funds to high-quality debt instruments with remaining maturities of no more than:
w: Correct: money market fund holdings are limited to debt with remaining maturities of not more than 13 months.
Wrong: six months is not the stated maximum remaining maturity for these funds.
Wrong: 90 days is shorter than the limit the chapter gives for money market fund holdings.
Wrong: five years is an intermediate-term horizon, far beyond a cash-equivalent fund’s permitted maturities.

questions.q: A customer plans to buy a home in about eight months and wants to park the down payment with safety, stability and high liquidity. Which type of fund fits best?
w: Correct: money market funds hold short-term, high-quality debt and aim for a stable $1 NAV with high liquidity.
Wrong: a sector fund concentrates in one industry and carries high risk, unsuited to short-term cash needs.
Wrong: high-yield bonds carry default risk and NAV volatility, which conflicts with the safety goal.
Wrong: small-cap growth stocks offer volatility and appreciation potential rather than stability.

questions.q: Mia invests $7,500 in a money market mutual fund whose NAV is holding at $1.00 per share and which charges no load. About how many shares does she receive?
w: Wrong: this would imply a share price of $100, far from the $1 stable NAV.
Wrong: this would imply a $10 share price, which is not how money market funds are priced.
Wrong: 75,000 shares would imply a price of $0.10 per share, which is not the stable NAV.
Correct: $7,500 ÷ $1.00 per share = 7,500 shares, since the fund aims for a constant $1 NAV and has no load.

questions.q: A client tells her representative that she holds a money market mutual fund and assumes it is FDIC insured because her bank sold it to her. What is the correct response?
o: It is insured up to $250,000 because a bank sold it
It is insured only if the sponsor is an FDIC-insured bank
It is not FDIC insured, and its $1 NAV is a goal that is not guaranteed
It is insured only for US individual investors
w: Wrong: the selling channel does not create FDIC coverage; money market mutual funds are never covered.
Wrong: even a fund sponsored by an insured bank is not itself covered by FDIC insurance.
Correct: money market funds are not covered by FDIC insurance and can break the buck below $1 per share.
Wrong: investor type is irrelevant; money market mutual funds are not FDIC insured for anyone.

questions.q: A retiree wants a stock fund that stresses steady dividend income over capital appreciation and may hold preferred, blue chip and utility stocks. Which fund type is most appropriate?
w: Wrong: sector funds concentrate in one industry and are not designed around steady income.
Correct: income stock funds invest in dividend payers such as preferred, blue chip and utility stocks.
Wrong: growth companies rarely pay dividends because they reinvest earnings into research and expansion, which conflicts with an income goal.
Wrong: small-cap funds seek greater appreciation with greater risk, not steady dividends.

questions.q: A high-net-worth investor in the highest federal tax bracket wants a bond fund whose interest income is free from federal income tax. Which fund is most appropriate?
w: Wrong: high-yield bond fund income is taxable and carries elevated default risk.
Wrong: corporate bond interest is taxable at the federal level, so it does not meet the tax goal.
Correct: municipal bond funds pass through interest that is free from federal income tax, suiting high-bracket investors.
Wrong: a growth stock fund is an equity fund that rarely pays dividends and is not a bond fund.

questions.q: A municipal bond fund pays a shareholder a dividend of $0.50 per share, representing tax-free interest, and a year-end capital gains distribution of $0.20 per share. Which statement about federal taxation is correct?
o: The dividend is exempt, while the capital gains distribution is taxable
Both distributions are exempt from federal income tax
The capital gains distribution is exempt, while the dividend is taxable
w: Correct: dividends reflecting muni interest are tax-exempt, but capital gains distributions remain taxable.
Wrong: the tax benefit of munis extends only to the interest income, not to capital gains.
Wrong: this reverses the treatment; interest is what the exemption covers.
Wrong: the muni interest dividend is exempt, so taxing both ignores the fund’s main benefit.

questions.q: Which type of mutual fund is the only one that is NOT actively managed?
w: Wrong: asset allocation funds have managers who shift the mix of stocks, bonds and cash as markets change.
Wrong: bond funds are professionally managed to select bonds that meet an income objective.
Wrong: sector funds are actively managed, concentrating on a chosen industry.
Correct: an index fund buys most or all securities of an index and is not actively managed after assembly.

questions.q: An investor says she wants one diversified fund in which a professional decides how much to hold in stocks, bonds and cash as conditions change. Which fund type best matches?
w: Wrong: an index fund passively replicates an index and does not shift among asset classes.
Correct: asset allocation funds combine stocks, bonds and cash, and the manager has discretion to adjust the mix.
Wrong: a money market fund holds only short-term debt and offers no stock or bond exposure.
Wrong: a sector fund concentrates in one industry rather than spreading across asset classes.

questions.q: A mutual fund has total assets of $480 million, total liabilities of $80 million and 20 million shares outstanding. What is its NAV per share?
w: Wrong: $480 million ÷ 20 million ignores the fund’s liabilities, which must be subtracted first.
Wrong: $560M ÷ 20M adds the liabilities instead of subtracting them.
Wrong: $4.00 is the liabilities per share ($80M ÷ 20M), not the net asset value per share.
Correct: ($480M − $80M) = $400M NAV; $400M ÷ 20M shares = $20.00 per share.

questions.q: A mutual fund’s NAV is $15.00 per share. It pays a distribution of $0.60 per share. Assuming no change in the market value of the portfolio, what is the NAV per share immediately afterward?
w: Correct: NAV falls by the amount distributed: $15.00 − $0.60 = $14.40 per share.
Wrong: a payout removes cash from the fund; it cannot raise the NAV per share.
Wrong: NAV does not stay the same, because cash leaves the fund when a distribution is paid.
Wrong: $14.00 subtracts more than the $0.60 distribution actually paid.

questions.q: Assuming the market value of the portfolio securities is unchanged, which of the following events would cause a mutual fund’s NAV per share to decrease?
o: The fund redeems a large block of shares
The fund pays a dividend to shareholders
The fund sells a large number of new shares
The sponsor sells shares to dealers at a discount
w: Wrong: cash paid out on redemption is offset by fewer shares outstanding, so NAV per share is unchanged.
Correct: a distribution sends cash out to shareholders without reducing share count, so NAV per share falls.
Wrong: cash coming in from new shares is offset by the new shares issued, so NAV per share is unchanged.
Wrong: dealer discounts affect the sponsor’s compensation, not the fund’s NAV per share.

questions.q: A customer enters an order to buy mutual fund shares at 4:45 pm on Wednesday. The fund calculates NAV at the 4:00 pm close each business day. At which price will the order be filled?
w: Wrong: filling at a close already passed is late trading, which is prohibited.
Wrong: mutual funds do not use opening prices; they are priced at the next calculated NAV.
Correct: forward pricing fills the order at the next NAV calculated after receipt, which is Thursday’s close.
Wrong: using an earlier NAV would give the customer a known price, which forward pricing prevents.

questions.q: A mutual fund has an NAV of $18.80 and charges a front-end sales charge of 6% of the public offering price. What is the public offering price?
w: Wrong: $18.80 × 1.06 applies the 6% to NAV, but the charge is a percentage of POP.
Wrong: $18.80 × 0.94 subtracts the charge from NAV, moving in the wrong direction.
Wrong: that is the NAV; the POP must exceed NAV when a sales charge applies.

questions.q: A mutual fund has an NAV of $24.00 and a public offering price of $25.00. What is the sales charge expressed as a percentage?
w: Wrong: $1.00 ÷ $24.00 divides by NAV, but a sales charge is always a percentage of POP.
Wrong: $1.00 is the dollar sales charge, not the percentage.
Wrong: 4.50% does not result from the figures given; the calculation yields 4.00%.

questions.q: A fund has an NAV of $47.50 and a sales charge of 5% of the public offering price. What is the dollar amount of the sales charge per share?
w: Wrong: $2.38 is 5% of NAV ($47.50 × 0.05), but the charge is based on POP, not NAV.
Wrong: $2.75 does not follow from either a NAV-based or POP-based calculation here.
Wrong: $5.00 is 10% of $50, double the actual charge.

questions.q:
Which of the following are characteristics of Class B mutual fund shares?

I. A contingent deferred sales charge
II. Breakpoint discounts
III. A 12b-1 fee higher than Class A shares
IV. A front-end sales load
w: Wrong: a front-end load is a Class A feature; Class B charges on redemption instead.
Wrong: Class B shares do not offer breakpoints; only Class A does.
Wrong: neither breakpoints nor a front-end load applies to Class B shares.
Correct: Class B shares carry a back-end CDSC and a higher 12b-1 fee than Class A, with no breakpoints or front load.

questions.q:
To charge the maximum permitted sales charge, a mutual fund must offer which of the following?

I. Breakpoints
II. Rights of accumulation
III. Automatic reinvestment of dividends at NAV
IV. A contingent deferred sales charge waiver
w: Correct: the three features are breakpoints, rights of accumulation and reinvestment of dividends at NAV.
Wrong: this leaves out reinvestment at NAV, the third required feature.
Wrong: this omits breakpoints and adds a CDSC waiver, which is not a required feature.
Wrong: a CDSC waiver is not one of the three required features, so including it is incorrect.

questions.q: A mutual fund offers breakpoints and rights of accumulation but does not allow shareholders to reinvest dividends at NAV. What is the maximum sales charge it may impose?
w: Wrong: the 8.5% maximum requires all three features, and this fund lacks NAV reinvestment.
Wrong: 4.50% is a sample tier in a breakpoint schedule, not a maximum sales charge.
Wrong: 5.75% appears in a sample breakpoint chart but is not the regulatory cap for this fund.
Correct: a fund missing any of the three features is limited to a maximum sales charge of 6.25%.

questions.q: A mutual fund wants to advertise itself as no-load. What is the maximum annual 12b-1 fee it may charge?
w: Wrong: 0.10% is below the actual cap; the permitted maximum is higher.
Wrong: 0.50% exceeds the 0.25% ceiling that applies to any fund advertising itself as no-load.
Correct: a fund calling itself no-load can charge a 12b-1 fee of no more than 0.25% of average net assets.
Wrong: 0.75% is the overall maximum 12b-1 fee for any share class, not the no-load cap.

questions.q: Which of the following expenses may a mutual fund pay out of its 12b-1 fee?
o: The fund’s marketing and distribution costs
w: Wrong: management fees are separate and are not covered by 12b-1 fees.
Correct: 12b-1 fees pay for the fund’s marketing and distribution (administrative) expenses.
Wrong: trading expenses on portfolio securities are not covered by 12b-1 fees.
Wrong: dividends are distributions of fund income to shareholders, not a 12b-1 expense.

questions.q: A mutual fund paid management fees of $1.8 million and other operating expenses of $0.7 million during a year in which its average net assets were $250 million. What is its expense ratio?
w: Wrong: $1.8M ÷ $250M counts only management fees and omits operating expenses.
Wrong: $0.7M ÷ $250M counts only operating expenses and omits management fees.
Wrong: 2.50 is the dollar total in millions; it was never divided by average net assets.
Correct: ($1.8M + $0.7M) = $2.5M; $2.5M ÷ $250M = 1.00% of average net assets.

questions.q: An investor puts $10,000 into a front-end load fund that has an NAV of $11.75 and a public offering price of $12.50. How many shares does the investor receive, assuming the entire $10,000 is the amount paid at POP?
w: Correct: investors pay the public offering price, so $10,000 ÷ $12.50 = 800 shares.
Wrong: $10,000 ÷ $11.75 uses NAV, but the investor’s payment buys shares at the higher POP.
Wrong: 750 does not result from dividing $10,000 by either price given.
Wrong: 1,000 would imply a $10.00 price per share, which does not appear in the facts.

questions.q: An investor plans to invest $300,000 in a fund family and hold the shares for many years. She wants the benefit of sales charge discounts for large purchases. Which share class is the best fit?
o: Any class, because all of them offer breakpoints
w: Wrong: Class C shares have no breakpoints and the highest annual costs, which grow the longer they are held.
Wrong: Class B shares do not offer breakpoints and carry higher 12b-1 fees, suiting investors with little cash.
Correct: Class A has a front-end load that suits long holders and is the only class offering breakpoints.
Wrong: only Class A shares offer breakpoints, so the classes are not interchangeable.

questions.q: An investor wants a short-term mutual fund investment and is willing to pay a level sales charge and relatively high annual fees. Which share class was designed for this kind of investor?
w: Wrong: Class A shares have front-end loads that are most beneficial for long-term holders and large purchases.
Correct: Class C shares carry a level load and high annual costs, designed for short-term investments.
Wrong: Class B shares suit investors with little cash and a long horizon, not short-term holders.
Wrong: closed-end funds have a single share class and no A, B or C structure.

questions.q: A fund’s Class B shares follow a typical CDSC schedule of 5%, 4%, 3%, 3%, 2% and 1% for years 1 through 6, then 0% from year 7 onward. What percentage applies to shares redeemed in year 5?
w: Wrong: 3% applies to years 3 and 4 on this schedule, not year 5.
Correct: reading the schedule year by year, year 5 carries a 2% contingent deferred sales charge.
Wrong: 1% applies in year 6, one year later than the redemption described.
Wrong: the charge only reaches zero in year 7 and beyond.

questions.q: A fund’s Class A schedule is: under $25,000, 5.50%; $25,000 to $74,999, 4.50%; $75,000 to $149,999, 3.50%; $150,000 and over, 2.00%. An investor makes a single $80,000 purchase. What is the dollar sales charge?
w: Wrong: $4,400 applies the top 5.50% rate, ignoring the breakpoint discount.
Wrong: $3,800 treats the tiers as incremental ($1,375 + $2,250 + $175), but breakpoints are not incremental.
Wrong: $3,600 applies the 4.50% tier, which is the bracket below the one that $80,000 reaches.
Correct: breakpoints apply to the whole purchase, so 3.50% × $80,000 = $2,800.

questions.q: A fund’s sales charge drops at $100,000. Which of the following is a breakpoint sale?
o: A representative recommends a $98,000 purchase to a client who has $120,000 to invest, in order to keep the higher commission
A representative recommends a $120,000 purchase and explains the discount
A client independently decides to invest $98,000 with no recommendation
A representative recommends exactly $100,000 after explaining the discount
w: Correct: steering a client to just below the breakpoint for a higher commission is the prohibited breakpoint sale.
Wrong: recommending an amount above the breakpoint with a clear explanation helps the client, so it is not a violation.
Wrong: without a recommendation by the representative, the client’s own choice cannot be a breakpoint sale.
Wrong: recommending exactly the breakpoint amount with disclosure does the opposite of steering the client below it.

questions.q: A fund’s schedule is: under $25,000, 5.50%; $25,000 to $74,999, 4.50%; $75,000 to $149,999, 3.50%; $150,000 and over, 2.00%. An investor signs a letter of intent for $150,000 over 13 months and makes a first purchase of $20,000. What is the dollar sales charge on that first purchase?
w: Wrong: $1,100 applies 5.50%, the rate that would apply to the first purchase alone without the LOI.
Wrong: $700 uses 3.50%, the bracket below the $150,000 promised under the LOI.
Correct: the LOI sets the rate by the promised total, so the 2.00% rate applies: 2.00% × $20,000 = $400.
Wrong: $900 applies 4.50%, which is the bracket for $25,000 to $74,999 and not the promised total.

questions.q: An investor signs a letter of intent to invest $100,000 over 13 months and receives a reduced sales charge, but invests only $70,000 by the deadline. What happens?
o: The LOI is automatically extended by 90 days
The investor receives a refund of the sales charge already paid
The fund liquidates escrowed shares to pay the higher sales charge that now applies
The investor keeps the lower sales charge on the $70,000 already invested
w: Wrong: 90 days is the backdating window for earlier purchases, not an extension of the commitment period.
Wrong: no refund is provided; the shortfall leads to a higher charge, not a reduction.
Correct: the additional shares bought with the reduced charge are held in escrow and liquidated to pay the higher charge.
Wrong: the lower rate depends on completing the commitment, so the otherwise applicable charge is collected.

questions.q: Which of the following counts toward completing a mutual fund letter of intent?
o: Appreciation in the value of shares already owned
Capital gains distributions reinvested in the fund
New cash purchases made within the letter-of-intent period
w: Wrong: share appreciation does not count toward LOI completion, unlike with rights of accumulation.
Wrong: reinvested dividends do not count toward completing an LOI.
Wrong: reinvested capital gains do not count toward completing an LOI, because only new purchases made in the window are credited.
Correct: only fresh purchases made during the 13-month period count toward the promised amount.

questions.q: Years ago a customer invested $23,000 in a fund. The position is now worth $31,000 because of market appreciation. The fund has a breakpoint at $30,000, and she invests another $2,000 with no letter of intent. What sales charge applies to the new $2,000?
o: The reduced rate, because rights of accumulation count appreciation
The full rate, because only the $23,000 of cash invested counts
The full rate, because rights of accumulation expire after 13 months
The reduced rate, but only if she backdates a letter of intent 90 days
w: Correct: under rights of accumulation the current value, including appreciation, is credited and new purchases get the lower charge.
Wrong: rights of accumulation can use share appreciation and reinvested dividends, not just cash invested.
Wrong: rights of accumulation have no time limit; the 13-month window belongs to a letter of intent.
Wrong: no letter of intent is needed, since rights of accumulation operate on their own.

questions.q:
Which of the following are features of rights of accumulation?

I. The discount applies to subsequent purchases, not the first transaction
II. There is no time limit
III. Share appreciation and reinvested dividends count toward the position value
IV. The commitment can be backdated 90 days
w: Wrong: this omits that appreciation and reinvested dividends count, which is a defining feature.
Correct: rights of accumulation reward later purchases, have no time limit, and count appreciation and reinvested dividends.
Wrong: backdating 90 days belongs to the letter of intent, and this answer also drops the first feature.
Wrong: the 90-day backdate is an LOI feature, and this pairing ignores the no-time-limit feature.

questions.q:
For purposes of reaching a breakpoint, which of the following may generally be combined?

I. A husband’s and wife’s investments in the same fund
II. A parent’s and minor child’s investments in the same fund
III. Investments in several funds within the same fund family
IV. An investor’s purchase and an unrelated friend’s purchase
w: Correct: spouses, minor children and funds in the same family can combine, while unrelated friends cannot.
Wrong: this leaves out combination purchases across a fund family, which are allowed.
Wrong: this excludes spouses, who may combine their investments in the same fund with the investor to reach a breakpoint.
Wrong: an unrelated friend’s purchase cannot be aggregated for the discount.

questions.q: An investor’s cost basis in a mutual fund is $5,000. She elects to reinvest $300 of dividends in additional shares. What is her adjusted cost basis?
w: Wrong: the reinvested dividends were already taxed, so they increase the basis rather than leaving it unchanged.
Correct: reinvested dividends are added to basis: $5,000 + $300 = $5,300.
Wrong: basis does not fall because of reinvested income; it rises by the amount reinvested.
Wrong: $5,150 splits the dividend in half, which has no basis in the rule.

questions.q: An investor bought 200 shares of a mutual fund at $12 per share and later 100 more shares at $18 per share. What is her average cost basis per share?
w: Wrong: $15.00 is the simple average of the two prices and ignores that more shares were bought at the lower price.
Wrong: $12.00 is the first purchase price only and ignores the later, higher-priced shares.
Wrong: $13.50 does not result from the cost and share totals.
Correct: total cost $2,400 + $1,800 = $4,200; total shares 300; $4,200 ÷ 300 = $14.00 per share.

questions.q: An investor owns 250 mutual fund shares bought at $8 and 150 shares bought at $16. Using average cost basis, she redeems 100 shares at $14. What is her capital gain on the redemption?
w: Wrong: $200 uses $12, the simple mean of the two prices, instead of the share-weighted average.
Wrong: $600 compares the sale price to the $8 first lot, which is not how average cost works.
Wrong: a loss of $200 compares the sale price to the $16 lot only, ignoring the average.

questions.q: A representative accepts a customer’s mutual fund purchase order at 4:20 pm and has it filled at the 4:00 pm NAV so that the customer can benefit from news released after the close. Which prohibited practice does this describe?
w: Wrong: switching involves moving a client between similar funds for no legitimate purpose.
Correct: filling an order received after the close at that day’s price instead of the next NAV is late trading.
Wrong: selling dividends is selling shares just before a payout, which is not what happened here.
Wrong: a breakpoint sale concerns purchases sized just below a sales charge discount level.

questions.q: A representative persuades a client to sell shares of a growth fund from one fund family and buy a growth fund from another family with nearly identical objectives, earning a new sales charge. This is an example of:
w: Correct: moving a client between similar funds for no legitimate purpose generates costs and taxes and is switching.
Wrong: rights of accumulation is a legitimate discount feature, not a violation.
Wrong: late trading concerns the timing of order pricing relative to the NAV calculation.
Wrong: forward pricing is the proper method for pricing fund orders, not a violation.

questions.q: A representative urges a client to buy a mutual fund two days before the fund pays a large dividend. Why is this practice prohibited?
o: The sales charge doubles when shares are purchased before a dividend
The fund would be unable to pay the dividend to a new shareholder
The dividend lowers NAV and creates a tax liability for the client, who gives up the chance to buy at the lower NAV
The dividend is forfeited by shareholders who purchase within five days
w: Wrong: the sales charge is not affected by the timing of a dividend.
Wrong: new shareholders do receive the dividend; the problem is the tax and the lower NAV.
Correct: the payout reduces NAV by the amount paid and is taxable, so waiting to buy after the distribution avoids the tax.
Wrong: no forfeiture rule applies, and the harm lies in the NAV drop and taxation.

questions.q: A client buys 1,000 shares of a mutual fund at $20.00 per share the day before the fund pays a $1.50 per share dividend. Ignoring market moves, how much taxable dividend income does the client receive?
w: Wrong: the dividend is taxable income even though NAV falls by the same amount per share.
Wrong: $20,000 is the amount the client paid, not the dividend.
Wrong: $18,500 is the value of the shares after the payout, not the dividend received.
Correct: 1,000 shares × $1.50 = $1,500 of taxable dividend income, while the shares drop to $18.50 each.

questions.q: After the initial public offering of a closed-end fund, how can an investor sell the shares?
o: Redeem them with the fund at NAV
Sell them to the sponsor at the public offering price
Only after the fund’s termination date
Sell them to another investor on an exchange
w: Wrong: closed-end funds do not redeem shares; redemption is a mutual fund feature.
Wrong: the sponsor does not repurchase closed-end shares at a public offering price.
Wrong: closed-end funds have no stated termination date that restricts selling.
Correct: closed-end shares trade investor-to-investor on an exchange, like stocks.

questions.q: All of the following are true of closed-end funds EXCEPT:
o: The fund charges an annual 12b-1 fee
Shares may trade at a discount to NAV
Investors pay a commission when buying or selling shares
The fund may issue preferred stock
w: Correct: closed-end funds do not charge sales charges or 12b-1 fees, so this statement is false.
Wrong: market supply and demand can push shares below NAV; this statement is true.
Wrong: closed-end shares trade like stocks, so commissions apply; this statement is true.
Wrong: closed-end funds may issue senior securities such as preferred stock; this statement is true.

questions.q: A fund has an NAV of $12.00 per share and a price to the public of $11.40 per share. Based on this pricing alone, what type of fund is it?
o: A mutual fund, because mutual funds can be offered below NAV
A closed-end fund, because only closed-end funds can be priced below NAV
Either a mutual fund or a closed-end fund
w: Wrong: mutual funds are offered at NAV plus any sales charge, never below NAV.
Correct: supply and demand allow closed-end shares to trade at a discount; a mutual fund cannot be priced below NAV.
Wrong: only the closed-end fund can sit below NAV, so the two cannot both be the answer.
Wrong: a no-load mutual fund is offered exactly at NAV, not below it.

questions.q:
A fund’s NAV is $30.00 per share and the price an investor pays is $30.00. Which of the following could the fund be?

I. A no-load mutual fund
II. A mutual fund with a front-end sales charge
III. A closed-end fund
w: Wrong: a closed-end fund can also trade exactly at NAV, so this omits a valid possibility.
Wrong: a mutual fund with a front-end sales charge is priced above NAV, so it is not consistent with the facts.
Correct: a no-load mutual fund is sold at NAV and a closed-end fund can trade at NAV; a front-end load would put POP above NAV.
Wrong: a front-end load would make the price exceed NAV, so item II cannot apply.

questions.q: A customer buys mutual fund shares for cash in a margin account on June 3. What is the earliest date the shares can serve as collateral for margin purchases?
o: They can never be used as collateral
w: Wrong: June 18 is only 15 days after purchase, short of the 30-day holding requirement.
Correct: shares acquire loan value after being held 30 days; June 3 plus 30 days is July 3.
Wrong: August 2 is 60 days later, far longer than the 30-day holding period.
Wrong: mutual fund shares cannot be bought on margin, but after 30 days they can act as collateral.

questions.q: A closed-end fund’s shares are trading 4% above its NAV. What best explains this?
o: The fund is required to redeem shares at a premium
The fund added a front-end sales charge
The fund did not calculate NAV that day
Investor demand for the shares is strong relative to the supply
w: Wrong: closed-end funds do not redeem their shares at all.
Wrong: closed-end funds charge commissions on exchange trades, not sales charges, so a sales charge cannot explain a premium.
Wrong: missing a NAV calculation does not itself create a premium; NAV need not be computed daily.
Correct: closed-end shares are priced by supply and demand, so strong demand can push the price above NAV.

questions.q: Which party handles custody of securities, recordkeeping for investors, and accounting and tax reporting for a unit investment trust?
w: Wrong: UITs do not have an investment adviser, since the portfolio is not actively managed.
Wrong: UITs have no board of directors; the trust is formed by the sponsor through the indenture instead.
Correct: the sponsor names a trustee in the trust indenture to handle these administrative duties.
Wrong: UITs have no corporate officers, so none of them could handle custody or recordkeeping for investors.

questions.q:
Which of the following describe a unit investment trust?

I. A fixed portfolio of securities
II. A termination date set at creation
III. Active management by an investment adviser
IV. Units that are redeemable with the trust
w: Correct: UITs hold a supervised fixed portfolio, have a set end date and redeem units, with no active manager.
Wrong: this leaves out redeemability of units, which is a UIT feature.
Wrong: UITs have no investment adviser, so item III is false.
Wrong: UITs are not actively managed, so item III disqualifies this choice.

questions.q: An investor wants a pooled product with known holdings that never change in style, a set end date tied to bond maturities and predictable monthly distributions. Which product fits best?
w: Wrong: a mutual fund is actively managed with a changing portfolio and no termination date.
Wrong: closed-end funds are actively managed and have no fixed termination date.
Correct: UITs have fixed portfolios, no style drift, a set termination date and predictable distributions.
Wrong: an asset allocation fund is managed and shifts its mix, so holdings are not fixed.

questions.q: An investor expects interest rates to rise sharply. Which of the following funds is most likely to suffer the largest decline in NAV?
w: Correct: bond fund values move inversely with rates, and longer average maturities mean greater NAV volatility.
Wrong: short-term bond funds are less sensitive to rate moves than longer-term funds.
Wrong: money market funds hold very short maturities and target a stable $1 NAV.
Wrong: cash-equivalent funds hold liquid short-term debt and are the least rate-sensitive.

questions.q: An investor in a unit investment trust needs cash several years before the trust’s termination date. How can she exit?
o: Sell the units on a stock exchange
Redeem the units with the trust, receiving a value based on the underlying holdings
Request that the fund create a new unit at NAV
She must wait; UIT units cannot be redeemed early
w: Wrong: UIT units are not traded in the secondary market.
Correct: units are redeemed with the trust at a price based on the current underlying value, which can be higher or lower than cost.
Wrong: new units of an existing trust are not created on demand, since units are offered only in the IPO.
Wrong: UITs are designed to be held but investors may redeem early.

questions.q: For a typical exchange-traded fund tracking an index, what usually causes its portfolio holdings to change?
o: The manager’s view that a stock is overvalued
A vote by the fund’s shareholders
A change in the composition of the underlying index
w: Wrong: ETFs are treated as passive vehicles and are not run on a manager’s market views.
Wrong: retail investors do not redeem with the fund; they sell on the exchange.
Wrong: shareholders do not vote on individual portfolio changes for an index-tracking ETF.
Correct: ETFs only change holdings when the index changes, a process called reconstitution.

questions.q: An investor wants index exposure with low costs and wants to place a limit order at midday. Which product fits best?
w: Wrong: mutual fund orders are priced at the next calculated NAV and cannot be limit orders during the day.
Wrong: asset allocation funds are actively managed and are not index trackers.
Wrong: UIT units are redeemable with the trust and do not trade on an exchange.
Correct: ETFs track an index at low cost and trade like stocks, allowing limit orders throughout the day.

questions.q: All of the following are features of exchange-traded funds EXCEPT:
o: A termination date fixed when the fund is created
Commissions paid on purchases and sales
Short selling and margin purchases are available
Market price set by supply and demand
w: Correct: ETFs do not have fixed termination dates, unlike UITs, so this is the exception.
Wrong: ETFs are exchange-traded, so commissions apply; this is a feature.
Wrong: ETFs allow short selling, margin and stop or limit orders; this is a feature.
Wrong: ETF prices fluctuate on supply and demand, so shares can trade at a premium or discount; this is a feature.

questions.q: Which of the following is a disadvantage of exchange-traded funds?
o: They cannot be purchased on margin
They carry higher management fees than actively managed funds
Their liquidity may encourage overtrading and increase commission costs
They cannot be sold during the trading day
w: Wrong: ETFs can be purchased on margin and sold short.
Wrong: ETFs generally have lower expense ratios because they are passively run.
Correct: easy liquidity can lead to overtrading and timing risk, and each trade carries commissions.
Wrong: ETFs trade throughout the day, which is an advantage rather than a disadvantage.

questions.q:
Which of the following trade on the secondary market during the day?

I. Mutual funds
II. Closed-end funds
III. Unit investment trusts
IV. Exchange-traded funds
w: Wrong: mutual funds do not trade on the secondary market; they are redeemed by the fund.
Correct: closed-end funds and ETFs trade intraday on exchanges, while mutual funds and UITs are redeemed.
Wrong: this wrongly includes mutual funds, which have no secondary market.
Wrong: UITs are not traded in the secondary market; they are redeemed by the trust.

questions.q: Which pair of investment company products is actively managed?
o: Unit investment trusts and exchange-traded funds
Mutual funds and unit investment trusts
w: Wrong: UITs and ETFs are supervised and passive rather than actively managed.
Correct: mutual funds and closed-end funds are management companies, while UITs and ETFs are supervised.
Wrong: UITs are not actively managed, so this pairing is incorrect.
Wrong: ETFs are passive vehicles, so only the closed-end fund in this pair is actively managed.

questions.q: Which of the following can an investor buy with borrowed funds in a margin account?
o: Shares of a no-load money market fund
Closed-end fund shares trading on an exchange
Shares of an index mutual fund
w: Wrong: mutual funds cannot be purchased on margin; the investor must pay 100% in cash.
Wrong: money market funds are mutual funds and so cannot be purchased on margin.
Correct: closed-end fund shares are exchange-traded and may be bought on margin.
Wrong: index mutual funds are still mutual funds and cannot be bought with borrowed funds.

questions.q:
Which of the following are components of a mutual fund’s total return?

I. Change in NAV
II. Dividend payments
III. Capital gains distributions
IV. The sales charge paid at purchase
w: Wrong: the sales charge is a cost of buying, not a source of return.
Wrong: this leaves out capital gains distributions, which are part of what the investor earns.
Wrong: this leaves out the change in NAV, which is the most important component.
Correct: total return combines the change in NAV with dividends and capital gains distributions received.

questions.q: An investor needs current income from a bond fund but has a low tolerance for changes in share value. Which fund is the best fit?
w: Correct: short-term bond funds provide income with less NAV fluctuation than longer-term funds.
Wrong: longer maturities pay more yield but cause the largest NAV swings when rates move.
Wrong: junk bonds carry default risk and volatility, the opposite of the investor’s tolerance.
Wrong: a sector stock fund is a concentrated equity fund, not an income-oriented bond fund.

questions.q: A mutual fund shareholder is said to hold an undivided interest in the fund. What does this mean?
o: Ownership of the specific securities the shareholder chooses
Ownership of a proportionate share of every security in the portfolio
A creditor’s claim for repayment of principal from the fund
The right to vote on each trade the adviser makes
w: Wrong: shareholders cannot pick individual holdings inside a pooled fund.
Correct: each share represents a proportionate slice of the entire portfolio.
Wrong: shareholders are owners of the fund, not lenders to it.
Wrong: the adviser makes trading decisions; shareholders do not vote on trades.

questions.q: Which feature is offered by mutual funds but NOT by closed-end funds, unit investment trusts or exchange-traded funds?
o: A continuous offering of new shares
w: Wrong: all of these pooled products spread money across many securities.
Wrong: each type of investment company states its objective.
Wrong: the other products are also affordable for small investors.
Correct: only mutual funds keep creating new shares; the others sell a fixed number of shares or units.

questions.q: Which investor is LEAST well served by a money market fund?
o: A saver who wants growth that outpaces inflation over 25 years
A buyer holding a down payment for a home purchase
An investor who needs to access cash quickly
A client who values price stability above all else
w: Correct: money market returns are relatively low and may not keep pace with inflation.
Wrong: safety and liquidity for a near-term purchase is the classic use.
Wrong: high liquidity is a main strength of these funds.
Wrong: a stable $1 NAV target serves this investor well.
